PACs

Premature atrial contractions occur when another region in the atria (other than the SA node) depolarizes before the SA node triggering a premature heartbeat

Premature atrial contractions (PACs), AKA Supraventricular ectopic beats (SVE), Supraventricular extrasystole (SVES), atrial premature complexes (APC) or atrial premature beats (APB)

Maxim Masiutin, CC BY-SA 4.0,via Wikimedia Commons

PACs have the following ECG characteristics:

The ectopic P waves appears sooner (premature) than the next expected sinus beats

The ectopic P waves may have a different shape and direction (because it is originating in a region other than the SA node)

The ectopic P waves maybe conducted through the AV node resulting in a NARROW QRS complex but if the PAC is premature enough, it would reach the AV node during its refractory period => not conducted

Maxim Masiutin, CC BY-SA 4.0,via Wikimedia Commons

Most PACs are conducted with typical QRS complexes but some may be conducted aberrantly through the infranodal system typically with a RBBB pattern

When the PAC occurs during the absolute refractory period it is not conducted

If two PACs occur in a row, they are called doublets and three PACs triplets and the rhythm is called atrial bigeminy, trigeminy, or quadrigeminy

If two PACs occur in a row and at a frequency of 100 or more beats/ min, it is called atrial tachycardia

Slide 6

Since the sinus node is often depolarized and reset, the interval between normal P waves before and after the PAC will not be twice the existing P to P interval , creating a shortest pause than a fully compensatory pause (unlike that seen after most premature ventricular contractions)

PACs

YitzhakNat, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Etiology

Idiopathic: diagnosed if other etiologies are excluded

Structural causes of PACs include coronary artery disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, left atrial appendage aneurysm, left ventricular hypertrophy, valvular heart disease, septal defects and Congenital heart malformation

Biochemical causes include sodium channel malformations and BMP2 mutations

Chemical causes incdeudde berta agonists, digoxin, chemotherapeutic drugs, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics, monoamine oxidase inhibitors and even beta blockers

Medical pathologies associated with increased incidence of PACs include MI, CHF, hypertension , DM, COPD, Coxasckie virus and higher CHA2DS2-VASC score

Also there is some states that predispose PACs such as anxiety , pregnancy, fatigue, alcohol and tobacco

Caffeine has not been associated with increased incidence of PACs (opposite to popular belief)

Diagnosis

Patients are often completely asymptomatic or sometimes they will describe a skipped beat or sudden fluttering or movement in the chest

PACs can be diagnosed using ECGs but mostly caught on Holter studies

Epidemiolgy

PACs are common the general population and increase with age

Over 99% of the general population will have at least one PAC in a 24 hour period

Many PACs can indicate increased risk of A fib and/or ischemic stroke

Treatment

Asymptomatic patients require no treatment

Symptomatic patients are treated by treating the underlying disorder or discontinuation of precipitating drug and reassurance

A beta blocker or Type 1A, type 1C or type III antiarrhythmic medication can suppress PAC, but given accordingly after careful consideration to their pro arrhythmic nature; attempts should be made to control PACs non pharmacologically first

In patients with refractory symptoms despite medical therapy or those with cardiomyopathy or heart failure linked to PACs, and those patients whom PACs trigger atrial arrhythmias like A Fib; further interventional therapy is indicated such as atrial pacing, catheter ablation of the PAC origin

Complications

PACs may lead to A Fib and ischemic stroke
